# [[1.0.0 P-119 — Badertdinov et al. 2025 — SWE-Rebench]]

- **Authors**: Ibragim Badertdinov, Alexander Golubev, Maksim Nekrashevich, Anton Shevtsov, Simon Karasik, Andrei Andriushchenko, Maria Trofimova, Daria Litvintseva, Boris Yangel (Nebius AI R&D team).
- **Venue / Year**: **NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track** (featured). arXiv:2505.20411 (May 2025, multiple revisions through 2025; v2 is the canonical NeurIPS camera-ready version).
- **URL**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20411 ; https://swe-rebench.com/ ; https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-Rebench (or successor repository under the SWE-bench organisation) ; HF dataset at https://huggingface.co/datasets/nebius/SWE-rebench.
- **Anchors**: PRIM-22 (Four Phases of Comprehension), PRIM-27 (Coverage-Guided Plateau Detection), PRIM-31 (Iterative Retrieval Refinement); the **continuously-evolving contamination-aware evaluation substrate** that the SWE-bench family (P-111, P-109, P-118) needs to keep its measured scores honest as model training cutoffs move forward.

SWE-Rebench is the **first SWE-bench-family benchmark whose freshness is a first-class property rather than a side-effect of when the dataset was curated**. Where [[1.0.0 P-111]] SWE-bench (the 2,294-instance original), [[1.0.0 P-109]] SWE-bench Verified (the 500-instance human-curated subset), and [[1.0.0 P-118]] SWE-bench Lite (the 300-instance fast-iteration subset) all freeze the task pool at a single curation date and then age out as model training cutoffs catch up to the instances, SWE-Rebench's pipeline **automatically harvests fresh tasks from GitHub on a rolling schedule** and **explicitly tracks each task's creation date against each candidate model's training cutoff**. The contribution decomposes into four complementary elements:

1. **Automated continuous task harvesting.** The SWE-Rebench pipeline periodically scans a configured set of active GitHub repositories (initially a Python-heavy ecosystem selection; SWE-Rebench V2, arXiv:2602.23866, generalises to a language-agnostic selection), identifies issues with verified fix commits that satisfy the original SWE-bench structural criteria (Python repository, failing-to-passing test transition, Docker-reproducible environment), and emits them as fresh benchmark instances. The pipeline replaces the "manually curated, frozen at publication" pipeline of [[1.0.0 P-111]] / [[1.0.0 P-109]] / [[1.0.0 P-118]] with a **continuously running evaluator** that admits new instances weekly and retires the oldest to keep the public leaderboard window bounded.
2. **Decontamination via training-cutoff provenance.** Every SWE-Rebench instance carries an explicit `created_at` timestamp and a per-model `training_cutoff` provenance flag. When the leaderboard scores a model, the leaderboard computes the **effective sample size** as the subset of instances whose `created_at` strictly post-dates the model's `training_cutoff`. A model cannot score against an instance whose commit predates its training; the leaderboard refuses to count that instance as a valid sample for that model. This is the **anti-leakage scaffolding** that distinguishes SWE-Rebench's "pass rate" from the older SWE-bench-family pass rates, where an unknown fraction of the leaderboard score could be attributed to the model having seen the GitHub commit during pre-training.
3. **21,000+ interactive Python task corpus with Docker-sandbox evaluation.** The initial SWE-Rebench release comprises **21,000+ interactive Python-based tasks** spanning hundreds of repositories, each backed by a Docker environment that supports the same `Agentless` / `SWE-agent` / `OpenHands` evaluation scaffolds that [[1.0.0 P-56]] Multi-SWE-bench established for multilingual evaluation. The Docker substrate means the benchmark inherits the deterministic reproducibility of the SWE-bench family; the scale means the benchmark can support **per-model training-cutoff partitioning** without the effective sample size collapsing.
4. **Quantified contamination inflation.** The headline empirical finding is that **several popular models score meaningfully lower on SWE-Rebench than on SWE-bench Verified**, with deltas of 5-15 percentage points on the same model against the same scaffold. The deltas are evidence that a non-trivial fraction of reported SWE-bench Verified pass-rates reflect **memorised pre-training exposure** to the upstream GitHub commits rather than generalisable code-repair capability. The deltas are largest for models whose training corpora are known to include large GitHub snapshots (closed-source frontier models trained through 2024); the deltas are smallest for models whose training corpora are explicitly GitHub-filtered or whose release predates the SWE-bench Verified curation.

**Why this matters for the SLM era**: SWE-Rebench's decontamination scaffolding is **the methodology MAgHARCM's internal benchmarks need** if any reported numbers are to be comparable across model releases. The 4B-30B SLM regime is particularly susceptible to contamination because (a) the open-source SLM training corpora often include GitHub snapshots with explicit deduplication, but the deduplication is rarely perfect at the commit-level granularity that SWE-bench evaluation requires, and (b) the small-model regime tends to memorise seen-and-fixed bugs more readily than the frontier regime (lower capacity → less generalisation between similar bug topologies). MAgHARCM's Validator's `ValidationReport.AllSuccess` metric needs the contamination-subtracted analogue to be a meaningful number when comparing Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct trained on Q1-2025 data against Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct trained on Q3-2025 data.

## Application in MAgHARCM

- **PRIM-22 (Four Phases of Comprehension)** — SWE-Rebench's contamination provenance tracking is the **Search-phase substrate** that the existing four-phase comprehension scaffold lacks. Where the current Comprehension agent retrieves code chunks from the repository under test, a contamination-aware Search agent would additionally **verify the chunk's git-blame provenance** against the model's training cutoff and **suppress chunks whose provenance window overlaps the model's training window**. This is the **per-instance provenance gate** that lets a MAgHARCM pipeline run on a model whose training is older than the benchmark's curation date without producing silently-contaminated scores.
- **PRIM-27 (Coverage-Guided Plateau Detection)** — the **continuously-evolving task harvest** is the substrate for plateau detection. Where the current Plateau Detection primitive watches for stagnation in the per-iteration pass-rate curve on a fixed benchmark, SWE-Rebench provides the **out-of-distribution diagnostic** that distinguishes "model has plateaued on the benchmark" from "model has memorised the benchmark". The two failure modes are observationally identical on a frozen benchmark; SWE-Rebench's continuously-evolving task pool is what makes them distinguishable.
- **PRIM-31 (Iterative Retrieval Refinement)** — the **per-instance provenance flag** is a new retrieval-refinement signal. The current Iterative Retrieval primitive refines retrieval by feedback from the LM (which chunks improve the LM's score on the current task); SWE-Rebench-style provenance lets the primitive additionally refine by **excluding chunks whose provenance overlaps the model's training window**. The two refinement signals are complementary: feedback-driven refinement catches chunks that confuse the LM in the moment; provenance-driven refinement catches chunks the LM might score artificially well on because it has memorised them.
- **Headline finding applied to MAgHARCM**: the 5-15pp contamination-inflation delta is the **first empirical evidence** that the SLM-era pass-rates MAgHARCM measures against [[1.0.0 P-111]] / [[1.0.0 P-109]] / [[1.0.0 P-118]] carry a non-trivial contamination floor. MAgHARCM's internal benchmarks should be **migrated to a SWE-Rebench-style contamination-aware substrate** for any number that is reported externally; the existing benchmarks remain the **fast-iteration calibration target** for in-sprint scaffold work where contamination is bounded by the in-sprint model's known cutoff.
- **Cross-reference**: P-119 anchors the **contamination-aware evaluation lineage** that supplements the existing SWE-bench family (P-111 / P-109 / P-118) with the time-axis dimension the static benchmarks lack. Add P-119 to PRIM-22, PRIM-27, PRIM-31 rows in `Software-Archaeology-Lineage.md`. This is the **fifth pillar** of MAgHARCM's evaluation substrate, sitting alongside [[1.0.0 P-111]] (full SWE-bench), [[1.0.0 P-109]] (Verified), [[1.0.0 P-118]] (Lite), [[1.0.0 P-56]] (Multi-SWE-bench multilingual extension), and [[1.0.0 P-120]] SWE-smith (synthetic-task generator).

## Hop-1 References (papers cited by Badertdinov et al.)

- Jimenez et al. (2024) — SWE-bench [[1.0.0 P-111]] (the Python-only predecessor; SWE-Rebench's direct parent pipeline).
- OpenAI (2024) — SWE-bench Verified [[1.0.0 P-109]] (the 500-instance human-curated subset; SWE-Rebench's contamination-aware scoring methodology is built on Verified's solvability filters).
- Jimenez et al. (2024) — SWE-bench Lite [[1.0.0 P-118]] (the 300-instance fast-iteration subset; SWE-Rebench's per-iteration cost model is calibrated against Lite's cost/iteration ratio).
- Zan et al. (2025) — Multi-SWE-bench [[1.0.0 P-56]] (the multilingual extension; SWE-Rebench V2's language-agnostic pipeline is built on Multi-SWE-bench's per-language issue-harvesting methodology).
- Yang et al. (2024) — SWE-agent [[1.0.0 P-112]] (one of the three canonical evaluation scaffolds that SWE-Rebench supports out-of-the-box).
- Wang et al. (2024) — OpenHands/CodeAct [[1.0.0 P-115]] (the multi-turn generalist scaffold that SWE-Rebench supports alongside the procedural Agentless scaffold and the tool-calling SWE-agent scaffold).
- Badertdinov et al. (2025) — SWE-Rebench V2 (arXiv:2602.23866) [INFERENCE: forward reference; V2 is the language-agnostic successor that extends the Python-only V1 pipeline to language-neutral task harvesting. Anchor as `[[1.0.0 P-119-v2]]` when the V2 paper note is materialised.]
